stories.title: Samsung bans smart TV apps that exposed users' internet connections to strangers
stories.summary: Samsung says it is banning smart TV apps found to be acting as residential proxy networks, secretly routing outside internet traffic through users' home connections without their knowledge, according to Engadget and TechCrunch. Separately, The Verge noted Samsung has discounted one of its smart monitors to $349.99, its lowest price yet, though that appears to be an unrelated promotion bundled into this coverage.
stories.whyItMatters: Proxy-style schemes hidden in ad-supported TV apps can expose users to security and even legal risk without their consent, and a major manufacturer cracking down signals wider scrutiny of what runs on smart TV platforms.
whatToWatch: Whether other smart TV makers announce similar app-vetting crackdowns
How Samsung enforces and communicates the ban to existing app developers
questions: Which specific apps were removed, and how many users were affected before the ban?

stories.title: AWS backs vibe-coding startup Superblocks, a sign of cloud giants courting AI-native dev tools
stories.summary: TechCrunch reports that Amazon Web Services is supporting Superblocks, a startup in the emerging 'vibe-coding' space, where developers build software largely through AI-driven, conversational tools rather than traditional programming. The report frames the involvement as carrying significant implications, though specifics on the scope of AWS's support aren't detailed.
stories.whyItMatters: Major cloud providers aligning with AI-coding startups could reshape how software gets built and which infrastructure providers capture that shift.

stories.title: Apple reportedly challenges UK government's renewed demand for iCloud backdoor access
stories.summary: According to a TechCrunch report, Apple is pushing back against a fresh UK government demand to build backdoor access into iCloud, reviving the long-running fight over encrypted user data. This follows earlier UK efforts to compel weakened encryption for law-enforcement access, though the specifics of this renewed demand aren't yet public.
stories.whyItMatters: The outcome could set a precedent for whether governments can force tech companies to weaken encryption on user data, with implications for Apple's global privacy stance and other cloud providers.
whatToWatch: Whether Apple again withdraws or alters an iCloud security feature in the UK
Any formal government statement or legal filing confirming the new demand
Reactions from privacy advocates and other major tech companies
questions: How does this renewed demand differ from the UK's earlier order that led Apple to pull Advanced Data Protection?
Could this dispute prompt similar demands from other governments?
